\label{def:ulm}
A collection $\mathcal{D} \subseteq \Cl{X}$ of closed subsets is \textbf{downward-closed} if $\emptyset \in \mathcal{D}$ and $\Cl{X} \ni A \subseteq B \in \mathcal{D}$ implies $A \in \mathcal{D}$. Let $\mathcal{D}$ be a downward-closed collection. A set $E \in \Cl{D}$ is \textbf{uniformly locally modeled on} $\boldsymbol{\mathcal{D}}$, or just \textbf{uniformly locally-}$\boldsymbol{\mathcal{D}}$, if there exists $\theta > 0$ (dependent on $E$, independent of $F$) such that for all finite $F \subseteq X$, $E \cap B_\theta(F) \in \mathcal{D}$. The collection of all such $E \in \Cl{X}$ is denoted \textbf{ulm}$\boldsymbol{(\mathcal{D})}$. The downward-closed condition implies $\mathcal{D} \subseteq \ulm{\mathcal{D}}$ and that $\ulm{\mathcal{D}}$ is also downward-closed. Also, whenever $\mathcal{I}$ is an ideal, $\ulm{\mathcal{I}}$ is an ideal. A downward-closed collection $\mathcal{D}'$ is \textbf{ulm-closed} if $\ulm{\mathcal{D}'} = \mathcal{D}'$. The \textbf{ulm-closure} of a downward-closed collection $\mathcal{D}$, denoted $\boldsymbol{\ulmc{\mathcal{D}}}$, is the intersection of all downward-closed, ulm-closed collections containing $\mathcal{D}$. It is easy to verify that $\ulmc{\mathcal{D}}$ is always itself downward-closed and ulm-closed.

It suffices to assume $v_n$ belongs to the dense subspace $\LFf{G} \subseteq \LF{G}$, and it suffices to find a norm null subsequence. Then we can find $N_2 > N_1$ large enough so that $\|T_{F_1,\theta}(v_{N_2})\| \leq 1$. Set $F_2 := F_1 \cup \supp{v_{N_2}}$.  By Proposition \ref{prop:T}, $T_{F_2,\theta}(v_n) \in \LF{G \cap B_\theta(F_2)}$. Thus, by definition of $\mathcal{D}$, $T_{F_2,\theta}(v_n)$ is norm null. Then we can find $N_3 > N_2$ large enough so that $\|T_{F_2,\theta}(v_{N_3})\| \leq 1/2$, and we set $F_3 := F_2 \cup \supp{v_{N_3}}$. Continuing in this way, we can find an increasing sequence of finite subsets $F_1 \subseteq F_2 \subseteq \dots \subseteq X$ and numbers $N_1 < N_2 < \dots$ such that $\supp{v_{N_i}} \subseteq F_i$ and $\|T_{F_i,\theta}(v_{N_{i+1}})\| \leq 1/i$ for all $i \geq 1$. We stress that the functions in $\Lip{\mathcal{I},X}$ are required to be globally defined on $X$ and not just on some set in $\mathcal{I}$. The subset $\Lip{\mathcal{I},X}$ is a subspace since $\mathcal{I}$ is an ideal. For each $p \in X$, we get a continuous linear functional $\delta_p \in \Lip{\mathcal{I},X}^*$ defined by $\delta_p(f) = f(p)$. For each subset $Y \subseteq X$, define $\boldsymbol{\LFf{\mathcal{I}}{Y}}$ to be the linear span of $\{\delta_p\}_{p \in Y}$ in $\Lip{\mathcal{I},X}^*$, and $\boldsymbol{\LF{\mathcal{I}}{Y}}$ its closure. We also stress that, despite the absence of `$X$' in the notation, the structure of the space $\LF{\mathcal{I}}{Y} \subseteq \Lip{\mathcal{I},X}^*$ depends not only on $Y$ but also $X$ because the functions in $\Lip{\mathcal{I},X}$ are required to be globally defined on $X$.

If $v \in \LFf{\mathcal{I}}{X}$, we denote by $\supp{v}$ the smallest finite set $F$ such that $v \in$ span$\{\delta_p\}_{p \in F}$. For the other inequality, it obviously suffices to assume $\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p} > 0$. Let $\varepsilon \in (0,\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p})$. Let $\mathcal{I}$, $Y$, $c$, $u$, be as above.

First we show that whenever $p,q \in X$ such that $d(p,q) > \rho(p,q) = c\cdot \min\{\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p},\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q}\}$, it holds that
\begin{equation} \label{eq:3c-1}
\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q} < 3c^{-1}d(p,q).
\end{equation}
Let $p,q$ be such points, and without loss of generality assume $\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q} \leq \rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}$. So then we have $d(p,q) > c \cdot \rad{\mathcal{I}}{q}$ and thus $2c^{-1}d(p,q)>2\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q}$. It is also an immediate consequence of the triangle inequality and the definition of rad${_{\mathcal{I}}}$ that $d(p,q) \geq \rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}-\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q}$. Adding these two inequalities, and using the fact that $c \leq 1$, gives us $\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q} < 3c^{-1}d(p,q)$.

Now, by Theorem \ref{thm:quotient}, there are $w \in \LF{Y}$ and $a \in \l{\mathcal{I}}{Y}$ such that $R_{\mathcal{I}}(w) + Q_{\mathcal{I}}(a) = u$ and $\|w\|+\|a\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{Y}} < 1$. $$\tilde{a} := a + \sum_{(p,q) \in Y^2: d(p,q) > \rho(p,q)} b_{(p,q)}(\mathsf{1}_p-\mathsf{1}_q).$$
The following estimate will show that $\tilde{a}$ is a well-defined element of $\l{\mathcal{I}}{Y}$ and moreover that $\sum_{(p,q): d(p,q) \in Y^2 \leq \rho(p,q)}|b_{(p,q)}|d(p,q) + \sum_{p \in Y} |\tilde{a}_{p}|\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p} < 3c^{-1}.$

$$\sum_{(p,q) \in Y^2: d(p,q) \leq \rho(p,q)}|b_{(p,q)}|d(p,q) + \sum_{p \in Y} |\tilde{a}_{p}|\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p}$$

\begin{enumerate}
\item \label{item:11} $c_\alpha \neq 0$ for all $\alpha \in A$,
\item \label{item:12} $d(p_\alpha,q_\alpha) < (\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p_\alpha}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q_\alpha})/2$ for all $\alpha \in A$,
\item \label{item:13} $\sum_{\alpha \in A} \|c_\alpha(\delta_{p_\alpha}-\delta_{q_\alpha})\| = \sum_{\alpha \in A} |c_\alpha|d(p_\alpha,q_\alpha) \leq 1$ and \\ $\sum_{\alpha \in A} \left\|c_\alpha(\mathsf{1}_{p_\alpha}-\mathsf{1}_{q_\alpha})\right\|_{\l{\mathcal{I}}{X}} = \sum_{\alpha \in A}, |c_\alpha|(\rad{\mathcal{I}}{p_\alpha}+\rad{\mathcal{I}}{q_\alpha}) \leq 2$

\end{enumerate}

The collection of all such indexed families is a poset under the relation $\{(c_\alpha,p_\alpha,q_\alpha)\}_{\alpha \in A} \leq \{(b_\beta,r_\beta,s_\beta)\}_{\beta \in B}$ if $A \subseteq B$ and for all $\alpha \in A$, $(c_\alpha,p_\alpha,q_\alpha) = (b_\alpha,r_\alpha,s_\alpha)$. This collection is obviously nonempty since it contains $\emptyset$ (and it is a set since we require the indexing sets to be countable ordinals). Every chain is bounded above by the union of the families in the chain. This union belongs to our poset since the four items above are all preserved under limits and items (\ref{item:11}) and (\ref{item:13}) and the fact that $p_\alpha \neq q_\alpha$ for all $\alpha \in A$ imply the indexing set must be countable. By Theorem \ref{thm:injective}, $R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{I}}$ is injective, so it remains to show \\ $\overline{R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{I}}(B_{\LF{\mathcal{J}}{X}})} \subseteq R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{I}}(7B_{\LF{\mathcal{J}}{X}})$. Suppose $v'_n \in\LF{\mathcal{J},X}$ and $R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{I}}(v'_n) \to u' \in \LF{\mathcal{I}}{X}$ with $\sup_n \|v'_n\|_{\mathcal{J}} < 1$ and $\|u'\|_{\mathcal{I}} < 1$. Let $c \in (0,1)$. Set $r_p := c \cdot \rad{\mathcal{J}}{p}$ for each $p \in X$. By Lemma \ref{lem:quotientfinite}, $u' = R_{\mathcal{I}}(w) + u$ for some $w \in \LF{X}$ and $u \in \LF{\mathcal{I}}{X}$ with $\|w\| + \|u\|_{\mathcal{I}} < 1$ and $\supp{u} \cap B_{r_p}(p)$ is finite for each $p \in X$. Set $v_n := v'_n - R_{\mathcal{J}}(w)$ so that $\sup_n\|v_n\|_{\mathcal{J}} < 2$ and $R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{I}}(v_n) \to u$. Then we apply Lemma \ref{lem:sequence2} with $r_p = r_p$, $u = u$, $v_n = v_n$, $c = c$ to obtain a sequence $\tilde{v}_n$ such that
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\|\tilde{v}_n\|_{\mathcal{J}} < 2$ for all $n \geq 1$,
\item $R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{I}}(\tilde{v}_n) \to u$,
\item \label{item:3} for all $p_i \in X$ and $n \geq i$, $\supp{\tilde{v}_n} \cap B_{cr_{p_i}}(p_i) \subseteq \supp{u} \cap B_{cr_{p_i}}(p_i)$.
\end{enumerate}
Fix $n \geq 1$, and set $Y := X \setminus (\cup_{i \leq n} B_{cr_{p_i}}(p_i))$ and $F := \cup_{i \leq n} (\supp{u} \cap B_{cr_{p_i}}(p_i))$ so that $F$ is finite and $\supp{\tilde{v}_n} \subseteq Y \cup F$. Choose $\varepsilon>0$ small enough so that $B_{\varepsilon}(Y) \subseteq X \setminus (\cup_{i \leq n} B_{c^2r_{p_i}}(p_i))$. Then Lemma \ref{lem:supp} implies
\begin{equation} \label{eq:supp}
\tilde{v}_n \in \LF{\mathcal{J}}{Z_n}
\end{equation}
where $Z_n := F \cup (X \setminus (\cup_{i \leq n} B_{c^2r_{p_i}}(p_i)))$.
Set $\rho(p,q) := c^3\min(\rad{\mathcal{J}}{p},\rad{\mathcal{J}}{q}) \leq c^2r_{p}$ and for each $j \geq 1$, $Z_{n,j} := B_{\rho(p_j,q)}(p_j) \cap Z_n$. When $n \geq j$,
\begin{equation} \label{eq:Znj}
Z_{n,j} = B_{\rho(p_j,q)}(p_j) \cap F \subseteq \supp{u} \cap B_{cr_{p_j}}(p_j).
\end{equation}

Suppose $\tilde{v}_n = \sum_{p \in X} c_{p,n}\delta_p$ and $u = \sum_{p \in X} c_p\delta_p$, so that $c_{p,n} \to c_p$ for each $p$. Since $\|\tilde{v}_n\|_{\mathcal{J}} < 2$, \eqref{eq:supp} and Lemma \ref{lem:quotientclose} allow us write
\begin{equation} \label{eq:c=b}
\sum_{p \in X} c_{p,n}\delta_p = \sum_{\substack{(p,q) \in Z_n^2 \\ d(p,q) \leq \rho(p,q)}}b_{(p,q),n}(\delta_p-\delta_q) + \sum_{p \in Z_n} a_{p,n} \delta_p
\end{equation}
with
$$\sum_{\substack{(p,q) \in Z_n^2 \\ d(p,q) \leq \rho(p,q)}}|b_{(p,q),n}|d(p,q) + \sum_{p \in Z_n} |a_{p,n}|\rad{\mathcal{J}}{p} < 6c^{-3}.$$
For the sake of notational convenience, we'll define $b_{(p,q),n} := 0$ if $(p,q) \in X^2 \setminus Z_n^2$ or $d(p,q) > \rho(p,q)$ and $a_{p,n} := 0$ if $p \in X \setminus Z_n$ so that the above equations remain true when the first terms are summed over $X^2$ and the second over $X$.

Fix a nonprincipal ultrafilter $\mathcal{U}$ on $\mathbb{N}$. It is easy to see that $|b_{(p,q),n}| \leq 6c^{-3}d(p,q)^{-1}$ and $|a_{p,n}| \leq 6c^{-3}\rad{\mathcal{J}}{p}^{-1}$ for all $p\neq q \in X$ and $n \geq 1$, and thus $b_{(p,q)} := \mathcal{U}\text{-}\lim_{n \to \infty} b_{(p,q),n}$ and $a_p := \mathcal{U}\text{-}\lim_{n \to \infty} a_{p,n}$ exist.
For each $p \in X$, evaluating each side of \eqref{eq:c=b} at the Lipschitz function $\mathsf{1}_p$ yields
$$c_{p,n} = \sum_{q \in X} (b_{(p,q),n}-b_{(q,p),n}) + a_{p,n}$$
$$=\sum_{\substack{q \in Z_n \\ d(p,q) \leq \rho(p,q)}} (b_{(p,q),n}-b_{(q,p),n}) + a_{p,n}.$$
Then for each $j \geq 1$, combining this with the definition of $Z_{n,j}$ gives
$$c_{p_j,n} = \sum_{q \in Z_{n,j}} (b_{(p_j,q),n}-b_{(q,p_j),n}) + a_{p_j,n}.$$
By \eqref{eq:Znj}, the set over which this sum is performed, $Z_{n,j}$, is eventually (depending on $j$) contained in the fixed finite set $\supp{u} \cap B_{cr_{p_j}}(p_j)$. Thus we can interchange the sum and $\mathcal{U}$-limit to obtain
$$c_{p_j} = \mathcal{U}\text{-}\lim_{n \to \infty} c_{p_j},n = \mathcal{U}\text{-}\lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{q \in X} (b_{(p_j,q),n}-b_{(q,p_j),n}) + a_{p_j,n}$$
$$= \sum_{q \in X} \mathcal{U}\text{-}\lim_{n \to \infty} (b_{(p_j,q),n}-b_{(q,p_j),n}) + \mathcal{U}\text{-}\lim_{n \to \infty} a_{p_j,n}$$
$$= \sum_{q \in X} (b_{(p_j,q)}-b_{(q,p_j)}) + a_{p_j}$$
and thus
$$u = \sum_{p_j \in X} c_{p_j}\delta_{p_j} = \sum_{p_j \in X} \sum_{q \in X}(b_{(p_j,q)}-b_{(q,p_j)})\delta_{p_j} + a_{p_j}\delta_{p_j}$$
$$= \sum_{(p,q) \in X^2}b_{(p,q)}(\delta_p-\delta_q) + \sum_{p \in X} a_p \delta_p$$
and
$$\sum_{(p,q) \in X^2} \|b_{(p,q)}(\delta_p-\delta_q)\|_{\mathcal{J}} + \sum_{p \in X} \|a_{p} \delta_p\|_{\mathcal{J}}$$
$$\leq \sum_{(p,q) \in X^2}|b_{(p,q)}|d(p,q) + \sum_{p \in X} |a_{p}|\rad{\mathcal{J}}{p}$$
$$= \sum_{(p,q) \in X^2}\mathcal{U}\text{-}\lim_{n \to \infty}|b_{(p,q),n}|d(p,q) + \sum_{p \in X} \mathcal{U}\text{-}\lim_{n \to \infty}|a_{p,n}|\rad{\mathcal{J}}{p}$$
$$\leq \mathcal{U}\text{-}\lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{(p,q) \in X^2}|b_{(p,q),n}|d(p,q) + \sum_{p \in X}|a_{p,n}|\rad{\mathcal{J}}{p} \leq 6c^{-3}$$
where the second to last inequality is Fatou's lemma. Thus, we set $v = \sum_{(p,q) \in X^2}b_{(p,q)}(\delta_p-\delta_q) + \sum_{p \in X} a_{p} \delta_p \in \LF{\mathcal{J}}{X}$, so the last two formulae give us $R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{I}}(v) = u$ and $\|v\|_{\mathcal{J}} \leq 6c^{-3}$. Then $R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{I}}(R_{\mathcal{J}}(w)+v) = R_{\mathcal{I}}(w) + u = u'$ and $\|R_{\mathcal{J}}(w)+v\|_{\mathcal{J}} \leq 1 + 6c^{-3}$. Taking $c \nearrow 1$ shows $\overline{R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{I}}(B_{\LF{\mathcal{J}}{X}})} \subseteq R^{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathcal{I}}(7B_{\LF{\mathcal{J}}{X}})$.
